1.1: 1.1 Argument. The Ephesians are Asians. These, having received the word of truth, persevered in the faith: the Apostle praises them, writing to them from the city of Rome, from prison, through Tychicus the deacon. Paul, an apostle. In his manner he puts the greeting first. Then he gives thanks to God, setting forth first the benefits bestowed on the human race, afterward those specially granted to the apostles themselves; then to the Ephesians themselves, showing by whom and to what they were called. Then he shows the dignity and primacy of Christ; afterward he invites them to patience and charity, commending the unity of faith and of the Church, and enumerating the gifts of grace. Finally, exhorting to the struggle against the princes of darkness, he describes the armor of Christian warfare. To all the saints. To the perfect, and not only to them, etc. To the faithful. Who, if not holy, are at least sound in the faith. Saints, by the exercise of virtues. And faithful, by the right faith which is in Christ Jesus. Rightly he put those two, for then a good life profits and is believed, if the faith is in Christ Jesus. Then they are truly holy if they are faithful in Christ. Or: distinguish between saints and faithful, so that you understand the saints as the greater and more perfect, the faithful as the less perfect.
1.3: 1.3 Blessed. The greeting having been set first, he begins with the giving of thanks, implying that all things are from God. He blessed. The word of blessing is one, but according to the fitness of the person it must be understood in various ways. God is blessed by man when he is extolled with worthy praises. Man is blessed by God when God imparts to him the gifts of his grace, not for his merits but by his mercy.
1.4: 1.4 As he chose, etc. Let no one therefore think that souls are eternal with God and had then merited anything, according to the error of those who say that before these visible things there were certain holy souls, and that they were therefore then chosen.
1.5: 1.5 Who predestined. Having set down the predestination that belongs to the justice and holiness of the present life, here another is set down belonging to eternal life, the effect of which he noted above.
1.6: 1.6 To the praise of the glory of his grace, etc. As if to say: The glory of the graces is the eternal adoption. In which he has made us gracious. The effect of the first preordination to justice. In the beloved Son. God the Father, loving his only-begotten, bestows the things of the Son upon those whom he loves and to whom he wills.
1.7: 1.7 In whom we have, etc. He shows a twofold grace, because he both redeemed us and did not impute our sins.
1.8: 1.8 Which has abounded. Thus far of what was given to the whole human race; now he speaks of what he gave singularly to the apostles.
1.10: 1.10 In the dispensation. That is, in the fullness of time dispensed by God, that is, in this time of grace, in which divine providence has reasonably dispensed to fulfill what was promised or prefigured in other times. For if men were wholly ignorant, not previously taught, they would not receive Christ, and unless they had first been convinced as proud by the natural and doctrinal law, they would think little of Christ's coming. To restore. AUGUSTINE. Those things in heaven are restored, etc., up to are renewed from the oldness of corruption. All things, which are in heaven. That is, the angels; or: to restore, that is, to fill up. Which are on earth. That is, men, who were depraved by sin. In him. That is, through Christ.
1.11: 1.11 In whom we also. Lest the apostles, in whom grace abounds, seem to have merited better than others, he shows that they were called as freely, not by merits, as others were. By lot. Grace is called a lot, because it is not man's choice but the will of God. Hence the Lord's tunic, woven from above, which signifies charity, came by lot. He works all things. Even to will the good, and that we begin to believe, that by our example no one may glory in man. For it is true: You did not choose me, but I chose you, etc. The praise of God's glory is when many are won to the faith, as the glory of a physician is when he cures many.
1.13: 1.13 In whom you also. Now he comes to what he gave to the Ephesians. When you had heard. Here he notes the cause and the time.
1.15: 1.15 Therefore. Having enumerated the benefits conferred on the human race, on the apostles, or on the Ephesians, the Apostle adds what he thinks of their benefits, namely that he gives thanks and asks that more be added, lest they become proud, but press on further.
1.17: 1.17 That God, etc. As if he said: To obtain it I do not plead merits, but that he is the God and Father of Christ, etc.
1.18: 1.18 The eyes of the heart. In his image, therefore, know its author, who is not reached by bodily sense. Do not think, then, that God is reached by bodily sense, but hear him with the eyes of the mind. In the body, where there are different members, you hear in one place, you see in another. But in your heart, where different members are not found, there you hear where you see. For this, then, may he enlighten the eyes. That you may know, etc. He says this that they may be more eager: because when they have fully learned what the fruit of believers is, they will become more eager in cultivating religion. Or thus: that hope be taken properly. And the sense is: That you may know what it is, namely his will, that is, how much avails the hope of eternal life to which he calls. And that you may know what is the fulfillment of that hope. Which he says thus: And what are the riches. Here he reveals what he understood by the name of hope: for he takes hope as the thing hoped for.
1.19: 1.19 What is the surpassing. The greatest teachers will have a certain increase of glory beyond what all will have in common. For all will have the same denarius. But star differs from star in brightness (1 Cor. 15). And there will be various dwellings in the Father's house (John 14).
1.20: 1.20 Raising him, etc. The example of the glory of the saints consists in the resurrection of the Savior, so that in it the faithful may know what has been promised to them. At his right hand. The right hand is eternal blessedness, which is given to the saints; the left is misery, which is for the impious. For God is not limited and enclosed by any form of body.
1.21: 1.21 Above every, etc. He says this on account of the incarnation of the Son of God, so that even made man he is said to be above all heavens and above every creature, having his name by nature, not by adoption.
1.22: 1.22 Under his feet, etc. By the feet full subjection is denoted, and all things are rightly subject to him, because they were made through him; or the feet signify the humanity, because as the foot is the lower part of the body, so in Christ the lower nature is the humanity, which even the angels adore. And him, etc. After recalling the dignity of Christ, he returns to us, showing that his dignity pertains to us; as if to say: God so exalted Christ that this exaltation of his pertains to us: because he is the head and we the body, that we may share with him. Head. According to the deity: because all were made by him; and also according to the humanity, by which the Church is joined to him, by nature and grace. For of his fullness we have all received (John 10).
1.23: 1.23 His fullness. Because he is filled up through them, yet being all in all both here and in the future. Likewise. When those who have entered into confession bend the knee to Christ, he is filled up, because those who depart seem to empty him. All in all. Because the members confer nothing on him, but he gives all to the members: for it is by his power that they are what they are.
2.1: 2.1 And you, when you were, etc. He recalls the former things, that they may be humbled in good things, and that it may be certain that if these things have been given to enemies, the things the apostle wishes will much more be given to friends; as if to say: He is head of the whole Church and of you, because he gave you life together: when, that is, although you were dead. Or we who have believed have hope of the inheritance, and you, namely, have believed. And God made alive, or raised Jesus, etc.
2.2: 2.2 The prince. Namely Beelzebub, who is prince of the malignant spirits, or, intransitively, prince of spirits. He calls the spirit of the air prince of error, in which he rules. Of the air. The murky air is the hell of the demons. Spirit. That is, of spirits: for the genitive singular is put for the plural. Who works in the sons of unbelief. What? Only his own evil works: and first and chiefly, since the very unbelief and infidelity by which they are enemies of the faith, through which he knows they could be cleansed?
2.3: 2.3 And we were by nature, etc. As if: Since these things were in us, let not the Gentile despair of becoming equal to the Jews. Children of wrath. Mortals are born with the wrath of God, because, Adam having sinned, the fault became ingrained as nature. For the human race was held under just condemnation, and all were by nature children of wrath.
2.5: 2.5 He made us alive together. Either us Jews and likewise you Gentiles, and this is: by whose grace you Gentiles are saved. And he raised up both together.
2.6: 2.6 He made us sit together, etc. Not emptily, but faithfully he already counts as done what he does not doubt will be. Certainly Christ already sits in the heavenly places, but we do not yet; but we hold it by sure hope.
2.7: 2.7 In the ages to come, abounding, etc. For in the age to come the gift of God will appear in the reward of believers; what eye has not seen nor ear heard. And these are the abounding riches, that so much is given as the mind cannot search out.
2.8: 2.8 And this not of yourselves, etc. Lest perhaps you say: I deserved it, therefore I received. Do not think you received by deserving. Grace preceded your merit: not grace from merit, but merit from grace. For if grace is from merit, you have bought it; you did not receive it freely. Grace precedes all merits, so that my merits may attain the gifts of God.
2.9: 2.9 Lest anyone boast. He does not say this because good works done with pious thought are made void, since God renders to each according to his works, and the glory of God belongs to him who does good, but because works are from grace, not grace from works. It is therefore good for man not to presume on the strength of his own will; because he who thought he could keep without his help what he had given, setting out into a far country and living prodigally, consumed everything: and worn down by misery, and coming to himself, said: I will arise and go to my father (Luke 15). Which good thought he would not have had unless the most merciful Father had inspired even that in him in secret.
2.10: 2.10 For we are his, etc. No one ought to boast, because we are created in faith and in works as his making, that is, his work, or we are created through his making, that is, his operation: and so one must not boast even of works through faith, since faith and all things are from grace.
2.11: 2.11 Wherefore. That you may know all things are from the grace of God. He had compared Jews and Gentiles, in that both had been under sin; now he shows that the Gentiles were less worthy and had endured the reproaches of the Jews, so that, now equal to the Jews, they are the more indebted to the grace of God. Once you. In some codices it is found written: who, there: you who were Gentiles, and according to this it is read in suspense up to: But now in Christ, etc.; the same sense, however, remaining.
2.12: 2.12 Guests. Hospes (guest) is as it were ostii pes (foot of the door), because when he was received into the house, the master of the house and the one received placed a foot on the threshold, and, hands having been given, he swore that he had entered peaceably.
2.14: 2.14 Who made both one. For he is the cornerstone, in which the two peoples, like walls coming from different corners, are joined to one another as in a kiss of peace. The wall. That is, the obstacle, on one side from the law, on the other from idolatry.
2.15: 2.15 Making peace, etc. He makes peace between them, that he may reconcile both to God the Father. In himself. Not otherwise than through the cross, that is, death, he slew the enmity that was between God and men, that is, he forgave sins. For the death of the Savior profited all.
2.17: 2.17 You were far off, etc. If you love God with affection, you are near; if you hate him, you are far. For no one is far from God by regions, but by affections.
2.19: 2.19 You are no longer guests. That is, less worthy in the faith, as those once received under the law. And strangers. That is, aliens from God. But you are fellow citizens. That is, of the same right and dignity in the house of God. Of the saints. Not of carnal Israel. And members of the household. That is, familiars. Of God. To whom he reveals secrets.
2.20: 2.20 Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone, etc. AUGUSTINE, on Psalm 86. Lest the Apostles or prophets (on whom the city is founded) hold themselves up, he follows and says: Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone; for in Christ the whole building rests as on the first foundation: which foundation is at the top, not at the bottom, as in a bodily structure.
2.21: 2.21 Grows into a holy temple in the Lord. No one is so perfect that he cannot grow.
3.1: 3.1 For this reason, etc. Having shown that peace and reconciliation were made through Christ, here he sets down through whom they themselves are built up together, because God revealed that salvation belongs to the Gentiles, and sent him to preach to them, and makes him suffer for them, that they may be the more grateful to God.
3.2: 3.2 If indeed you have heard. That is, if you have understood the grace, that is, the apostleship dispensed by God, who knows why he chose me for this office? Or the apostleship, through which we weigh out different things to different people. By this he wishes them to know that by God's judgment he was sent by Christ to preach to the Gentiles the mystery of the grace of God.
3.3: 3.3 As I wrote above, etc. Namely, there: He himself is our peace. For there he briefly touched the sum of the mysteries revealed to him in a short discourse, not so much bringing forth all that he knew as showing it from a little.
3.5: 3.5 And to the prophets. The earlier prophets foresaw long ago this concerning the Gentiles, that they were to be called and would be partakers of God's gift, but this lay hidden, that without the law salvation would be theirs through faith in Christ.
3.6: 3.6 Through the Gospel, etc. Through preaching the gift of God is known, which God gives to the Gentiles according to the working of his power: by which he raised Christ, in whom all are saved without works of the law.
3.7: 3.7 Minister. For it is not mine but God's, and so no thanks are to be given to me, but to God.
3.8: 3.8 Unsearchable. By nature, that is; but through grace and the revelation of the Holy Spirit they are searchable to the faithful.
3.9: 3.9 Hidden from the ages. In the world are hidden the rational causes of all things which come about naturally, as Levi was hidden in the loins of Abraham when he was tithed. But in God are hidden the causes of those things which are done by grace, or of those which are done wonderfully and not naturally to signify this, which were done by the ministry of angels. In God. For God has hidden in himself the causes of certain deeds, which he did not instill in created things, and he fulfills them, not by that work of providence by which he established natures that they might be, but by that by which he governs as he wills the things which, as he willed, he founded. There too is the grace by which sinners are saved. For man is restored not by nature depraved by vice but by the grace of God.
3.10: 3.10 That it may be made known. It was given to me to evangelize and to enlighten. See how great this is, since by it something was added to the angels, who learned many secrets in these things. In the heavenly places. Because there the Church was first, where after the resurrection this Church too is to be gathered, that we may be equal to the angels of God.
3.11: 3.11 According to the foreordaining. For the wisdom which in its nature is simple is manifold according to the things done in the world, which God predetermined, that is, preordained, since it is varied in manifold ways. And lest the teachers of the sacred page seem to contradict themselves in the aforesaid statements, what was said can be determined thus: that to those who are of greater dignity, and through whose ministry those things were announced, they were known in part, for instance to those familiars and messengers; but to those of lesser dignity they were unknown.
3.14: 3.14 For this cause. I ask you, and I beseech God, that grace may work with you. And this is what he adds: For this cause. In which he shows they have the choice of their own will. But lest they think that sufficient, he adds: I bow my knees to the Father. In the Greek only this is found; but what has been added in the Latin codices, of our Lord Jesus Christ, fits well, because he was praying that we may obtain by the merit of him whose Father he is properly and by nature, not by adoption.
3.15: 3.15 Fatherhood, etc. Neither angel nor man is truly a father as God is, who is father of all, by creation, and by the re-creation of the faithful, whom he adopted as sons. Or it is named, that is, is nameable. For from him who is father of all, both the angels in heaven and men on earth received that they should call others fathers. And note that Christ, the only-begotten of God by nature, signifies by the benefit of adoption that he is a father, saying: Son, your sins are forgiven you (Matt. 2). Likewise the Holy Spirit, by whom the just are adopted as sons. A man is called a father either by nature, or by the authority of example, or by reason of benefit.
3.17: 3.17 In charity. I pray also that you be rooted, that is, firmly planted, from the likeness of a tree, which the deeper it is fixed in the earth, the more it grows and yields richer fruit.
3.18: 3.18 With all the saints. This is the communion of the heavenly commonwealth. These do not seek their own, but the things of Christ, that is, they do not pursue private advantages, but take counsel in the communion where the salvation of all lies. What is the breadth. Of charity, which ought to be extended even to enemies, and to do good with cheerfulness, because he who gives sadly loses what he gives. There is need, then, of breadth of charity, lest whatever good you do perish. But because with iniquity abounding the charity of many grows cold, there is need also of length. And height. Of charity. This is that the heart be directed upward, that God be awaited as the reward. For if you do good even to enemies, and give cheerfully, you have breadth; and if you persevere in these to the end, you have length. But if you do all these things not for the heavenly reward, it has no height: and so there will be now neither breadth nor length. For to have height is to think of God, to love God, and to love him freely as helper, as crowner, finally to count himself the reward, to expect nothing other than himself. If you love, love freely. If you truly love, let him whom you love be the reward. And depth. Of charity, that is, that you may be able to understand the hidden judgment of God; why he gives to this one, but not to that. For from the depth of God's judgments, which we cannot search out and contemplate, proceeds everything that we can do. What I can, I see; whence I can, I do not see, except that I know it is from God. But why he gives to that one and not to this one, it is far beyond me, it is an abyss and a depth. Now, then, charity itself is exercised in good works to help others, and extends even to enemies; and this is breadth. Now by long-suffering it endures adversities, and perseveres in what it has truly held; and this is length. This whole it does to obtain the eternal homeland, which is promised to it on high; and this is height. But that charity arises from what is hidden, and this is depth.
3.19: 3.19 That you may be filled. Because then nothing is lacking to the Christian, when he thus knows the Father and the Son. Otherwise the profession of the deity is not whole, because faith is neither whole in the Father alone nor perfect in the Son alone. Unto all the fullness of God. Not that they be (full God) as some in error wished, but that they be perfectly full of God; or thus: that by confession and thanksgiving, as to the Father, so also to the Son, honor be reserved, and all things that are from God the Father be believed to be made and restored through the Son, so that there may be a full profession of divinity in believers.
3.20: 3.20 Able to do all things, etc. In this there are certain things which no one else would ask or understand, such as that God, as man, would die for men, and other things of this kind.
4.1: 4.1 I beseech. Thus far he has shown that all things are to be attributed to grace; from here he admonishes about morals, first all in common, afterward each order individually.
4.2: 4.2 In charity. AUGUSTINE. For this is the action of the right road, which always has its eyes on God. Such action is neither broken by business, nor turbulent, nor crippled, nor bold, nor fleeing, nor headlong, nor prostrate.
4.3: 4.3 In the bond of peace. That is, keeping peace. This peace is, if we tolerate until the last harvest the sins which cannot be uprooted without harm to the wheat or with hope of the salvation of those to be corrected.
4.5: 4.5 One Lord. You must keep unity, because we have one Lord, not three, for whose diverse wills you would have to be at variance. And you are commanded to believe the same and to work in the same way. And you have one God, creator of all and father by providing: and therefore no one can prefer himself to another. Which God is above all, that is, surpasses all creatures, whose dignity should invite you, and through all, diffused, because everywhere, and therefore to be feared, since he can nowhere be escaped. And in us all, by grace, who keep unity. And so this is taken not singularly of one person but commonly of all, that is, of the Trinity. One faith. Not in number but in kind, because it is alike in all.
4.8: 4.8 He led captivity captive. That is, those whom the devil had made captive from paradise, and had made the property of the world and of hell, Christ made captives again, while they are led back to heaven.
4.11: 4.11 Prophets. AMBROSE. In the New Testament, prophets are called the expounders of the Scriptures, though there were some at the beginning of the faith who foretold the future, like Agabus and the seven daughters of Philip. Evangelists. Who are also deacons, because even if not priests, they can evangelize.
4.12: 4.12 For the work of the ministry. He gave these for the work of the ministry, that each may fully do the work of the ministration entrusted to him. For if one had everything, he would not do each thing perfectly. For the perfecting. That is, that he may perfect those who are already holy. And for the building up. That is, that they may build into the body of Christ those who are still alien.
4.13: 4.13 Until. That is, on the day of judgment. We all. Who are in one and not discordant faith: and in one and not differing unity of knowledge of the Son of God; or in the virtues by which the Son of God is known in us; or by which we shall know him in the future. We meet. Each other from the different parts of the world, or Christ himself, running as it were in desire to joy. Unto a perfect man. That each may be a perfect man and have the same age, which is the measure and limit of age, beyond which nothing naturally grows in man: in which age Christ had the fullness of years and of body, in which he passed from this world. For all will rise in the same age in which Christ died and rose, whatever age they died at.
4.15: 4.15 Christ. He is called Anointed. And in the Old Testament kings were anointed.
4.17: 4.17 This therefore. He admonishes them to beware of the custom of old paganism; as if he said: Because God has given so many aids for the keeping of unity, and because you can grow and will meet him, I say this, I do not beseech as before.
4.18: 4.18 Darkened. Not a little: and therefore it is less wonderful if they walk in vanity rather than you who are enlightened and have hope of life. From the life of God. There are two lives: one of the body, the other of the soul; and as the life of the body is the soul, so the life of the soul is God: and as if the soul leaves, the body dies, so the soul dies if God leaves. The soul departing from the light of justice, the more it seeks what it may find against justice, is the more repelled from the light of truth, and sinks into darkness.
4.19: 4.19 Past feeling. Or without pain, which is drawn from the Greek, that is, not grieving over sin.
4.21: 4.21 As the truth. He says this because there are some in the Church who under the name of Christ do not follow the truth which Christ taught.
4.22: 4.22 Put off. He does not command that the body be put off, but that life be changed for the better. The old. Some think that the old man is the body and the new the soul; but the body is the outer man, the soul the inner: and in the inner this oldness and newness takes place.
4.23: 4.23 In the spirit of your mind. The Apostle did not wish two things to be understood there, as if the mind were one thing and the spirit of the mind another, but because the mind is spirit. Similarly it is said: In the putting off of the body of the flesh, that is, of the flesh which is the body. The mind, then, or reason, or intelligence, is the image of God, by which man is set over the rest: who, created in the knowledge of God, after he lost his taste by sin, is renewed in the same, that the image may begin to be reformed by him by whom it was formed.
4.24: 4.24 Who is created according to God. For he was conceived in the virginal womb, by the work of the Holy Spirit from the seed of a woman without the seed of a man. This was new; hence Jeremiah: The Lord will do a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the lap of her womb (Jer. 31).
4.25: 4.25 Wherefore. He pursues the parts of the old and the new man. With his neighbor. Even a Gentile: because every man is a neighbor by the condition of first birth, or by hope of conversion every man should be thought a neighbor.
4.26: 4.26 Be angry, that is, be indignant at yourselves with such vehemence that you cease to sin, because upon this anger the sun of justice does not set, but rather shines upon it. Anger is a natural movement of the mind against those who sin; but lest by exceeding measure you sin by rebuking too harshly. Hence Solomon: Do not be overly just, for he perishes by his justice (Eccl. 7). Justice must therefore be tempered, whence God also bears with the wicked, that some of them may be corrected. Let not the sun go down. He wishes anger not to last, because if it lasts, occasion is given to the devil. For the angry man thinks evil, and so the devil inserts himself to bring about evils. Let not the sun go down. Let Christ not leave the mind, who never dwells with anger.
4.27: 4.27 Do not, etc. There are two gates by which the devil enters: desire and fear concerning earthly things. With these turned the opposite way God enters. The former are to be closed, the latter opened.
4.29: 4.29 Let no speech, etc. In the servant of God all things ought to appear good, nor should his purity be stained in any part.
4.30: 4.30 And do not grieve. By disobedience, the Holy Spirit, that is, the preacher of truth, which is to grieve the Holy Spirit as far as you are concerned. Which you ought not, in whom you were as it were sealed like wax with his image left to you; or you were sealed, that is, set apart from the wicked.
4.31: 4.31 All bitterness. Even if these things happen from attending causes, yet they must be tempered. Blasphemy. Blasphemy is that by which false things are said about God himself. And therefore it is worse to blaspheme than to perjure, because in perjuring God is called as witness to a false thing; but in blaspheming, false things are said of God himself.
5.2: 5.2 For a fragrance of sweetness. If Christ's death was a sweet fragrance to God, then he gladly accepted his death. Did those who crucified him not sin, then? But it is not so, because they unjustly killed the just man; he was offered by the will of the Father and his own. So also Judas, what does he have but sin in betraying Christ? Yet unless Christ had betrayed himself, Judas would not have betrayed him. Judas betrayed Christ, Christ betrayed himself. But the one was doing the business of his selling, the other of our redemption. Therefore the one sinned impiously, the other acted mercifully.
5.5: 5.5 The covetous. He equates avarice with idolatry, because he signifies as covetous the man whose god is money, or because the things of God, which God wishes to serve the needy, he usurps for himself and stores away, and prefers to God, as idolatry does with the honor of God.
5.6: 5.6 Empty words. All their reasonings are empty words, void of fruit, drawing to punishments.
5.9: 5.9 For the fruit, etc. Works of this kind are the fruit and the work of light. And justice, etc. Justice and truth are parts of goodness. And the sense is: In all goodness and justice and truth. That is, speak things just and true fittingly.
5.11: 5.11 Reprove. With a gentle mind, as the Apostle says elsewhere. Do this, namely, that outwardly the rebuke sound terrible, and within the love of gentleness be held. He joins two things, namely that they not share by consenting, and that they reprove. For in these two ways the wicked man does not stain you, if you do not consent and if you reprove. The Apostle embraced both, saying: Do not have fellowship, etc., that is, do not consent, praise, and approve. And because it is little not to consent, he adds: But rather reprove, that is, rebuke, correct, restrain. And the sense is: Do not be consenting to evils by approving them, nor negligent by not reproving, nor proud by reproving insultingly.
5.13: 5.13 But all things. As if: Even if it is shameful to say what they themselves do, yet they must be reproved, because thus they are often made manifest through confession and penance: and therefore they must be reproved, because what is thus made manifest is turned into light; or those wicked are made manifest to themselves that they are wicked, and therefore must be reproved, because so they begin to be light. For everything that is made manifest. That is, the wicked man, when he comes to know himself to be wicked, becomes light. Is light. That is, through penance he begins to be turned to good.
5.14: 5.14 Arise. Through confession. And rise up. Through satisfaction.
5.16: 5.16 Redeeming the time. That is, what you have done too little in one time, restore in another, halving the days which the impious do not halve. For some halve, some fill up the days, some do not even begin; that is, some die in Egypt, some in the desert, some in the holy land. Nor is it wonderful if you have done too little, since the days are evil and not everything can be done at will.
5.21: 5.21 Subject to one another. Not only hearers to prelates, but also prelates to subjects, serving them in charity and humbly taking care. For even if the dignity of superiors is real, it is yet administrative; hence the Apostle: I have made myself the servant of all (1 Cor. 9). It is therefore the part of superiors (their dignity remaining) to serve, as it is the part of inferiors to obey humbly; and this ordered subjection, of superiors as well as inferiors, ought to be in the chaste fear of Christ, who commanded humility.
5.22: 5.22 Wives. Thus far he has dealt with morals in common; now he urges certain things on each order.
5.27: 5.27 Not having spot, etc. Because by good action she is clean from spot, and by hope stretched to heavenly things: hence his garment on the mountain shone white like snow, which signified the Church cleansed of every spot of sin, which by Christ's extension on the wood of the cross has been stretched free of wrinkle, and by desire for heavenly things. Not having spot now, or wrinkle, but that she be holy, here by good works, and without blemish, in abstinence from evil. Or this will be in the future, for then the Church will be holy by glory and without blemish by the removal of corruption. As Christ shed his blood to wash away the spot of the Church, and stretched himself on the cross to remove the wrinkle, so husbands too, if need be, ought to die to save their wives, and instruct them with the word of life, that they may present them to God.
5.29: 5.29 For no one ever. He who prefers, therefore, to be without a body hates not the body but its corruptions and weight. As Christ also the Church. Let the husband do so for his wife, who is his flesh: because so Christ too nourishes the Church with the food of his body, and cherishes her with the spiritual garments of precepts, virtues, and good works.
5.32: 5.32 This is a great sacrament. Lest anyone think it is in husband and wife, according to the coupling of each natural sex and the bodily mingling, he adds: I speak in Christ, etc. According to this, therefore, as in Christ and the Church, what was said is taken: They are no longer two, but one flesh, and as bridegroom and bride are spoken of, so head and body. Whether, then, head and body is said, or bridegroom and bride, understand one thing. For out of two there is made as it were one person, namely out of head and body, out of bridegroom and bride: which wonderful and excellent unity Isaiah commends, in whom Christ speaking says: As a bridegroom he has bound a mitre on me, and as a bride he has adorned me with ornament. The sacrament of this spiritual unity was that which in Genesis is said literally of the union of marriage.
6.2: 6.2 First. Namely among the commandments that concern man on the second table. For the Decalogue pertains to two precepts of charity, of God and of neighbor. To the first precept, of God, three strings pertain, that is, three commandments, because God is a Trinity. To the other precept, namely of the neighbor, seven strings, that is, seven commandments. And those three pertaining to God were written on the first table. And the other seven, to the neighbor, on the second table. Among these this is rightly first, because as God is principally the origin of man, so the father is secondarily. To this commandment is added a promise, which is not found in the others.
6.5: 6.5 Servants, obey. Servitude began from sin; for the first cause of servitude is sin, so that no man was subjected to man by the bond of condition, which was not except by God's judgment, with whom there is no iniquity, and who knows how to distribute different punishments to the merits of offenders. In simplicity. He makes servitude free; not by deceitful fear but by faithful love, until iniquity passes away and all power is made void.
6.10: 6.10 Finally. After the special precepts by which he admonished the individual orders, he now admonishes all in common; as if: Thus far I have helped you by word and deed; henceforth, in the future, in the remaining time, by faith and love.
6.12: 6.12 Rulers of the world. They are not so called because they rule the world, which consists of heaven and earth; but he calls sinners the world, of which John says: And the world did not know him (John 1). Such a world they rule, against whom we have perpetual enmity: because what we suffer from importunate men, they do. For they instigate and inflame them and move them as their vessels, and touch them like instruments. Against them we have a hidden struggle, for which the Apostle arms us. Of darkness. Lest the demons be thought to rule this visible world, he adds what he understood by the name of world: Of this darkness, that is, of sins; as if: The demons do not rule the world which consists of heaven and earth, but sinners. Against spiritual. As if: The enemies are to be feared because spiritual and invisible, and because wicked: and they fight not for a small thing but to take away the heavenly inheritance. By heavenly things he means the virtues, in which we suffer the demons' battle; or the wicked spirits are in the heavenly places, that is, in this lower air. For they fight as horsemen on men as horses. Let us kill the horsemen, then, and possess the horses.
6.14: 6.14 Having your loins girded, etc. That is, restraining carnal concupiscences with the belt of chastity, not by pretense but in truth, or through charity. Having put on the breastplate of justice. Rightly it is compared to a breastplate of justice, because as a breastplate is woven of many rings, so justice consists of many virtues. Otherwise: justice can be compared to a breastplate because as a breastplate protects the chest, binds the belly, and guards the thighs, so justice repels superfluous thoughts which are wont to turn in the breast: it binds the gluttony of the belly and suppresses luxury as well.
6.15: 6.15 Shod. Mark says the apostles were shod with sandals or soles, so that the foot be neither upright nor bare toward the earth, that is, neither the Gospel be hidden nor rest on earthly comforts. Feet. That is, let the affections be fortified with virtues lest they be pricked by vices, so that they may be ready to preach the Gospel which announces peace between God and man; or that they may be ready to fulfill the precepts of the Gospel.
6.16: 6.16 The shield of faith. Faith is the shield, under which justice is safe, as under the protection of all the virtues, which is held out before all the weapons and which the devil attacks first of all.
6.17: 6.17 And the helmet. The helmet is eternal salvation, the memory of which wraps the mind that it not fail. And the sword of the Spirit. The word of God is a two-edged sword, teaching of temporal and eternal things. Promising the consolation of the former in the Old Testament, the perfection of the latter in the New. For what is promised us temporally belongs to one edge of the sword, what is promised forever to the other. Therefore also they are called two Testaments, because the Old promises earthly things, the New eternal. Of this sword the Lord says: I came not to bring peace on the earth, but a sword (Matt. 10). This sword is truly sharp, because it divides the one whom it has made from the world.
6.18: 6.18 In the Spirit. He prays in the Spirit who prays with a clean conscience and whole faith. He prays in the flesh who, with a polluted mind, sins again, not by chance but by purpose.
6.19: 6.19 For the opening, etc. That is, that I may openly unlock the mystery of the Gospel, that is, the secrets of the incarnation and passion. As if: Lest the pressure of tribulation, by fear itself, blunt the edge of teaching.
6.23: 6.23 Peace to the brethren. He wishes them peace, which is the gate of love.
